chunks: "The ground on a chip varies because ground isn't a perfect zero-ohm, zero-inductance node.
It's metal, so it has resistance and inductance, and whenever current flows through it, you get a voltage drop. There are a few main mechanisms.
The biggest one for digital chips is inductance. When several outputs switch at once, they dump charge into the die's ground, and that current changes quickly.
It flows out through the bond wires or bumps, pins and vias to the board, which have maybe a few nanohenries in total, so V equals L di over dt lifts the on-die ground above board ground.
That's ground bounce, and it's worse with more outputs switching, faster edges, and fewer ground pins. Second is plain IR drop.
The on-die power grid, package traces and board planes have resistance, so a chip that draws amps sees its local ground and supply sag relative to the regulator, especially far from the pins.

Third, shared return paths and coupling: noisy circuits and sensitive ones sharing the same return path, substrate noise on a mixed-signal die, ground loops between boards, and ESD or other transients that inject current into ground.
The practical fixes are more ground pins and low-inductance packages like flip chip, decoupling capacitors right at the die, slower edges, and solid ground planes with good return paths.
And the effect matters because everything is measured relative to ground, so if the chip's ground moves, thresholds, ADC references and clocks all see errors."
